# Introducing Aielia Write

## The problem that started it all

We used to draft in a chat tool, copy the text into a word processor, and shuttle changes between the two. Every revision meant re-pasting the draft so the model could see what had changed. Paragraphs drifted out of sync, and it became hard to tell which parts were AI-written and which version was current.

## Why existing tools were not enough

Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Notion AI all draft well, but in our experience none of them kept a source behind a claim or flagged it when that source changed. Jenni AI looked like the closest fit, but it is aimed at academic papers, with citation styles and a literature database most writers do not need. The blogging tools we looked at optimize for search rankings, not for whether what you wrote is true.

## What Aielia Write does

Aielia Write is built on Aielia, our system for tracking facts. It pulls out each claim in your draft sentence by sentence, checks each one against your sources, and keeps a record of which passages back it. Every chat edit can be undone, because a version is saved before any change. You bring your own key, and your articles stay on your own computer, with a spend meter and a cap.

## Getting started

Aielia Write does not run models of its own, so it needs an API key from a model provider. We suggest OpenRouter, which gives you one key that reaches models from many providers. Set a spending limit before you start, and you cannot be surprised later.

chat.text: Which claim in this article is the one a reader is most likely to challenge?

The claim a reader is most likely to challenge is **"your articles stay on your own computer"** in the "What Aielia Write does" section.

The article also says Aielia Write runs no models of its own and needs your API key from a provider such as OpenRouter. Claim-checking and chat edits go through that provider, so your draft text has to leave your machine. A careful reader will notice this within a few paragraphs, and privacy is a topic people watch closely. The article's own review notes already flag this section as not fitting the rest.

Two close runners-up:

- **"Set a spending limit... you cannot be surprised later."** A cap limits spend but doesn't guarantee there are no surprises, so it overpromises. This is also flagged for review in the article's records.
- **The competitor comparison.** The claim that Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Notion AI don't keep a source behind a claim has no source in the article's records. Jenni's page, as provided, says "every claim traceable to the source," so a reader could push back on the idea that this is a gap only Aielia Write fills.

What I could and couldn't verify:

- **Based on the article and its records:** the contradiction on local storage and the flagged review items. These come from the article text and its review notes, not from outside checking.
- **Based on the supplied excerpts only:** the Jenni quote and the OpenRouter details. Both pages were cut off, so I haven't seen their full content, and I didn't read them fresh. To check, open jenni.ai and openrouter.ai directly.
- **Not verified at all:** what Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Notion AI or the blogging tools actually do with sources, and how Aielia Write actually stores data or sends text. To check, look at each tool's current docs and at Aielia Write's own storage and network behavior.

The simplest fix for the first claim is to say that draft text is sent to your chosen model provider, while the articles and version history are stored locally, assuming that's true of the product.

**What the Jenni excerpt you supplied shows**
- The page title calls it an "AI Academic Writer & Research Tool for Students & Academics," and the tagline describes a workspace where researchers "read, write, and cite." That fits "aimed at academic papers."
- The excerpt shows a library of 5,032 sources with Cite buttons. That fits the "literature database" part.

**What I could not verify**
- **Citation styles.** The excerpt shows citing but never names styles such as APA or MLA. It was also cut off, so they may appear elsewhere on the site.
- **The live page.** I'm relying on the excerpt you supplied, not a fresh read of jenni.ai. The site may have changed, or may say more than the excerpt does.
- **Your judgment calls.** "Looked like the closest fit" and "most writers do not need" are opinions, so no link will prove them. Presenting them as your view, as "in our experience" does elsewhere in the section, is the honest framing.

**How to check:** open jenni.ai and look at its features and pricing pages for citation styles and the source library.

**Ways to resolve the comment**
1. Link jenni.ai where Jenni is first mentioned.
2. Keep "citation styles" only if the site confirms it. Otherwise soften it to "citations and a literature library."

Jenni's tagline, "every claim traceable to the source," may also draw a reader's attention. The article says none of the four general-purpose tools keep a source behind a claim, and a reader who clicks through to Jenni will see it advertises something similar. Consider acknowledging that, for example by saying Jenni's traceability is built for academic work.
